How to take a reading that means something

Push the probe in slowly to about two-thirds of the pot's depth, where the roots are, and wait a few seconds for the needle to settle. Take two or three readings in different spots — the edge of a pot often reads drier than the middle — and use the lowest one for drought-tolerant plants and the highest for moisture-lovers. Wipe the probe dry and store it out of the soil; leaving it in corrodes the tip and drifts the readings.

Cheap probe meters measure electrical conductivity, not water directly. Soil with lots of fertilizer salts reads wetter than it is; very peaty or bark-based mixes read drier. That is why the chart pairs every zone with a finger-test equivalent — calibrate your meter against your finger for the first few weeks, then trust the number.

What the readings mean

Most consumer soil moisture meters use a 1–10 scale with three marked zones. If yours uses 1–4 or a color band, map it to these zones.

ReadingZoneFinger test equivalentWhat to do
1–2DrySoil is dry two or more inches down; pot feels lightWater cacti, succulents, snake plant, ZZ now
3Dry side of moistTop inch dry, slightly cool and damp belowWater most tropical foliage — pothos, monstera, ficus
4–5MoistTop inch just starting to dryWater calathea, peace lily, ferns; wait on everything else
6–7MoistSoil damp at the surfaceWait, including moisture-lovers — unless a fern or maidenhair
8–10WetWater beads on the surface or saucer is fullDo not water; empty the saucer; if it stays here, check drainage

Targets are typical ranges, not rules. A plant in a bright warm window dries faster and will tolerate a lower reading; the same plant in a dim corner should be watered higher on the scale to avoid sitting wet.

How to use this sheet

  1. Print the PDF and keep it with the moisture meter.
  2. Cross out plant groups you do not own; add your own plants in the blank rows with a target reading from the chart.
  3. Each time you check a plant, write the date and the reading. Mark Watered? only if the reading was at or below the target.
  4. After a few weeks, look at the gap between watering dates for each plant — that is its real interval, which you can copy to a watering schedule sheet.
  5. If a plant reads wet for more than a few days after watering, note it: the pot may lack drainage or the roots may be rotting.

Questions

Is this sheet really free?

Yes. The PDF is free to download and print — no sign-up, no email, no watermark.

What is a good moisture level for indoor plants?

It depends on the plant. Cacti and succulents should fall to 1–2 on a 1–10 meter before watering; most tropical foliage to about 3; ferns and calathea should stay in the 4–6 moist zone. The chart lists ten common groups.

Do I need a moisture meter?

No — the finger test works, and the chart shows the equivalent. A meter helps with deep pots, plants you cannot easily reach into, and for anyone who tends to water too often and wants a number instead of a feeling.

Why does my meter read differently from the chart?

Scales differ by brand, fertilizer salts raise readings, and bark or peat-heavy mixes lower them. Use the zones (dry, moist, wet) rather than exact numbers, and check your meter against the finger test at first.
